title: Foreign Investors Pump ₹84,290 Crore Into Indian Stocks in November's First Fortnight
excerpt: After pulling ₹70,704 crore out in September and October, FPIs returned in nine straight sessions as AI stocks sold off globally, crude fell 13% and large-caps looked cheap — but strategists call the turn tactical, not structural.
body:
• Foreign portfolio investors put a net ₹84,290 crore into Indian equities between November 2 and 13 — nine trading sessions — reversing two straight months of outflows, depository data reported by PTI shows.
  • The buying follows withdrawals of ₹34,843 crore in October and ₹35,861 crore in September, and cuts cumulative FPI outflows for 2026 to about ₹2.1 lakh crore, from nearly ₹3 lakh crore a few weeks ago.
  • Analysts credit a global AI-stock sell-off, a 13% first-week drop in Brent crude to about $97 a barrel, and cheaper large-cap valuations; financials, telecom, capital goods, pharma and autos led the buying.
  • For investors, the strategists' caution matters: Trackk's Vedant Gupte calls it "a sharp tactical turn, not yet a structural return" — most buying went into index heavyweights.

Foreign investors have come back to Indian equities in size. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) made a net investment of ₹84,290 crore in Indian shares during November 2-13, the first fortnight of the month, covering nine trading sessions, according to depository data reported by PTI and carried by The Hindu BusinessLine.

The inflow is a sharp reversal. FPIs had withdrawn ₹34,843 crore in October and ₹35,861 crore in September. Even after November's buying, foreign investors remain net sellers for 2026 overall — but the cumulative outflow has narrowed to around ₹2.1 lakh crore, from nearly ₹3 lakh crore a few weeks earlier.

"November's foreign buying is a sharp tactical turn, not yet a structural return. Falling crude and money rotating out of the crowded Asian AI trade have pushed FPIs to close an extreme underweight on India, and most of that buying has gone into index heavyweights."

— Vedant Gupte, Co-Founder and CEO, Trackk

What drove the turn

The trigger, analysts say, was a sell-off in global AI-linked stocks that pushed investors to look beyond technology-heavy markets. Falling crude helped India's case directly: Brent declined around 13 per cent in the first week of November to nearly $97 per barrel, easing the import-bill and inflation concerns that had weighed on Indian assets. Attractive valuations in select large-cap stocks, easing geopolitical concerns and improved visibility on domestic earnings added to the pull, Rohan Goyal, investment research analyst at MIRA Money, told PTI.

Sector-wise, financials, telecom, capital goods, pharmaceuticals and automobiles saw aggressive buying, according to VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments, who also pointed to short-covering in frontline large-cap stocks — particularly leading banking names — as a factor behind the Nifty's move above the 25,000 mark. Some power stocks also gained on strong earnings.

Debt flows and what to watch

Foreign money also came into Indian debt, in smaller size: ₹7,815 crore through the Fully Accessible Route and ₹1,167 crore through the general route, against a withdrawal of ₹702 crore through the Voluntary Retention Route, the depository data showed.

Whether the equity buying holds is the open question. Gupte noted that even after the buying spree, FPIs have recovered only a small portion of this year's withdrawals, while domestic institutional investors have been using the rally to book profits. Dheeraj Gaur, chief investment strategy officer at Choice Wealth, said markets will now track the US Federal Reserve's minutes, crude prices amid Iran-Gulf tensions, the rupee, expectations around the RBI's rate decision, the remaining second-quarter earnings, and whether the Nifty can sustain levels above 25,000 — alongside how the global unwinding of the AI trade develops. For NRI investors watching from abroad, the practical read is the strategists' shared one: the money is real, but it is positioned as a trade, not yet a homecoming. The earnings test now under way — the subject of our look at whether Indian IT stocks' October rally survives their results — will help decide which it becomes.
